title: The Prideful 3
content:
After rubbing the ring for a moment, Jiang Cheng forced himself to pull back his lingering hostility.

He was furious, but as a Clan Leader, he had to weigh the bigger picture. He couldn't afford to be as hot-headed as a kid like Jin Ling. Ever since the decline of the Qinghe Nie Sect, the balance of power among the Three Great Sects had tipped: the Lanling Jin and Gusu Lan clans shared a deeply intimate alliance due to the personal friendship between their sect leaders, effectively leaving Jiang Cheng and his Yunmeng Jiang Sect isolated on the board. Lan Wangji, Hanguang-jun, was a cultivator of immense renown, and his elder brother, Zewu-jun Lan Xichen, was the reigning Clan Leader of Gusu Lan. The Twin Jades of Lan had always been thick as thieves. If Jiang Cheng could avoid tearing the diplomatic veil completely, it was better not to make an open enemy of them.

On top of that, Jiang Cheng’s sword, Sandu, had never crossed blades with Lan Wangji’s Bichen; there was no telling who would come out on top. Though Jiang Cheng held his family’s heirloom ring, Zidian, Lan Wangji’s guqin, Wangji, was just as terrifyingly renowned. The one thing Jiang Cheng could never stomach was losing ground, and without absolute certainty of victory, he wasn't about to draw against Lan Wangji.

Jiang Cheng slowly withdrew his hand from the ring. Lan Wangji had clearly decided to meddle here, and continuing to play the villain would look cheap. I'll settle this tab later. Having run the calculations, Jiang Cheng turned to glance at Jin Ling, who was still glaring furiously while clutching his sealed lips.

“If Hanguang-jun wants to punish you, take your lumps,” Jiang Cheng sneered. “It's not every day a master goes out of his way to discipline another clan's junior.”

His tone dripped with sarcasm, though it was impossible to tell who was catching the stray. Lan Wangji never stooped to petty verbal sparring and simply treated the barb like empty air.

Jiang Cheng’s words carried thorns, pivoting on a dime as he snapped at the boy: “What are you still standing around for? Waiting for the beast to throw itself onto your blade? If you can’t bag whatever’s haunting Dafan Mountain tonight, don't bother coming back to me!”

Jin Ling shot Wei Wuxian a venomous glare, though he didn't dare test the man who had actually struck him mute. Sheathing his sword, the boy offered stiff formal bows to both elders, hoisted his bow, and retreated into the woods.

Lan Sizhui stepped forward. “Sect Leader Jiang, the Gusu Lan Sect will compensate you in full for the destroyed Deity-Binding Nets.”

Jiang Cheng let out a cold bark of laughter. “Keep it!”

Pivoting, he marched down the slope in the opposite direction. The guest disciples scrambled to trail behind him in terrified silence, their faces long, already bracing for the brutal tongue-lashing awaiting them back at camp.

Once their silhouettes dissolved into the timber, Lan Jingyi couldn't help venting: “What is Sect Leader Jiang’s problem?!”

The moment the words slipped out, he remembered the Lan Clan’s rules—Do not speak ill of others behind their backs—and snapped his mouth shut, shrinking back under a terrified glance toward Hanguang-jun.

Lan Sizhui offered Wei Wuxian a gentle smile. “Young Master Mo, we meet again.”

Wei Wuxian’s lips gave a faint, awkward twitch.

Lan Wangji spoke up, his instructions stripped clean of decorative fluff: “Get to work.”

Snapping back to reality, the juniors remembered why they’d climbed Dafan Mountain in the first place. Shaking off the distraction, they stood at attention, respectfully waiting for any final pointers.

After a beat, Lan Wangji added, “Do your best. Do not push beyond your limits.”

His voice was low, laced with a calm, magnetic resonance that could make your heart skip if you were standing too close. The juniors chorused their obedient assents and hurried off into the deeper woods, not daring to linger.

Watching them go, Wei Wuxian mused that Jiang Cheng and Lan Zhan really were night and day. Even their parting words to their juniors were polar opposites. Just as the thought crossed his mind, Lan Wangji turned and offered him a nearly imperceptible nod.

Wei Wuxian blinked in surprise.

Ever since their youth, Lan Wangji had been impossibly, rigidly upright—stiff as a board, completely humorless, unable to tolerate even a speck of dirt, and fiercely opposed to Wei Wuxian walking the crooked path. Sizhui had undoubtedly briefed him on "Mo Xuanyu’s" suspicious antics back at Mo Village, yet here was Lan Wangji, offering a silent gesture of gratitude to acknowledge his role in saving the kids.

Caught off guard, Wei Wuxian reflexively returned the bow. By the time he straightened up, Lan Wangji’s white-clad back had already dissolved into the night.

After a lingering pause, Wei Wuxian turned and headed down the mountain trail.

Whatever quarry was lurking on Dafan Mountain, he couldn't touch it now. Wei Wuxian could steal from anyone in the world, but he would never steal from Jin Ling.

It was actually Jin Ling.

Out of all the countless scions in the Lanling Jin Sect, he’d managed to run straight into Jin Ling. Had he known, how could he have ever thrown that filthy taunt in the boy's face—“You’ve got a mother to birth you, but no mother to raise you”? If someone else had dared say that to Jin Ling, Wei Wuxian would have made sure they learned the bloody definition of watching their tongue.

Yet the mouth that said it was his own.

Standing motionless beneath the dark canopy, Wei Wuxian wound up and slapped himself across the face.

Smack.

The strike cracked through the clearing, leaving his right cheek burning hot. A nearby thicket rustled, and the spotted donkey poked its head out, blinking at him. Wei Wuxian let his hand fall to his side.

For once, the stubborn beast didn't kick; it ambled over and nudged him gently. Wei Wuxian gave one of its long ears an affectionate tug, managing a crooked, self-deprecating smile. “You wanted to play the hero saving the damsel, but you stuck me with the dirty work.”

While the donkey grunted its complaints, a fresh wave of cultivators came hiking up the ridge. With the four hundred Deity-Binding Nets slashed to ribbons by Lan Wangji’s flying blade, the folks who had been dithering at the foot of the mountain were swarming back up the slopes. Since every one of them was technically Jin Ling's competition, Wei Wuxian briefly weighed the idea of beating them back down the hill, but decided against it, quietly stepping aside into the shadows.

The mismatched crowd chatted as they hiked, venting as they went: “That little young master of the Jin Clan… Both the Jin and the Jiang families have spoiled him rotten. He’s this arrogant and tyrannical at his age—if he ever takes the helm of the Lanling Jin Sect, how are the rest of us supposed to survive?!”

Wei Wuxian slowed his pace, listening.

A soft-hearted cultivator sighed. “Can you really blame them for indulging him? The poor boy lost both his parents before he could even form memories.”

“Junior Sister, that’s no excuse. Plenty of people lose their parents young, but if everyone acted with his brand of rotten manners, the world would burn!”

“Though to be fair, Wei Wuxian was a monster to do what he did. Jin Ling’s mother was Jiang Cheng’s own sister, the shijie who practically raised Wei Wuxian with her own two hands.”

“Jiang Yanli truly died in vain, raising an ungrateful viper like that. And Jin Zixuan had it even worse—just because of some petty, old friction with Wei Wuxian, he ended up in an early grave.”

“Did Wei Wuxian ever not pick a fight with someone…?”

“Right? Aside from that pack of rabid corpses he leashed, did you ever hear of him getting along with a single living soul? Enemies at every turn, universally despised—even he and Hanguang-jun couldn't stand the sight of each other, constantly at each other's throats like oil and water.”

“Speaking of which, we really owe Hanguang-jun for tonight…”

Wei Wuxian walked on in silence until the bubbling murmur of a creek caught his ear.

He hadn't passed this water on the trek up. Realizing he’d taken a wrong turn somewhere along the dark trails, he’d wandered off onto a secluded path.

Leading the donkey by its tether, he stepped up to the water’s edge. The moon hung high in the sky, unobstructed by the canopy, fracturing into ripples of frost-white light along the current. Looking down, Wei Wuxian caught sight of a distorted face shimmering on the water's surface.

He slammed a palm down, shattering the clownish reflection into spray. Scooping up handfuls of freezing creek water, he aggressively scrubbed away the caked powder and rouge.

When the ripples settled, the reflection revealed an exceptionally refined young man. He looked clean and luminous, as if washed clear by moonlight—gentle brows, bright eyes, with the faint ghost of a natural upward curve at the corner of his lips. Yet as he stared down at himself, drops of creek water clinging to his lashes dripped into the current, looking strikingly like falling tears.

It was a young, unfamiliar face. It wasn't Wei Wuxian, the Yiling Laozu who once turned the mortal realm upside down and bathed in storms of blood.

He stared at the stranger in the water for a long time, rubbed his eyes dry, and sat heavily on the grassy bank.

It wasn't that he couldn't handle people dragging his name through the dirt. Back when he’d chosen this path, he’d known exactly what kind of hell he was walking into. He had constantly reminded himself of the Yunmeng Jiang clan's motto: Attempt the impossible.

He’d always told himself his heart was forged from iron. But at the end of the day, iron rusts, and flesh still bleeds.

The little spotted donkey seemed to pick up on his mood. For once, it didn't throw a braying fit; after standing quietly beside him for a minute, it flicked its tail and trotted off toward the trees. Wei Wuxian stayed slumped by the bank, unmoving. The donkey looked back, stomped its hooves, and seeing no reaction, ambled begrudgingly back to clamp its teeth onto Wei Wuxian's lapel, tugging persistently.

Moving or sitting made no difference to him anyway, and since the animal had resorted to biting, Wei Wuxian let himself be led.

The donkey pulled him over to a small grove and began circling a patch of tall weeds. Lying in the grass was an abandoned Qiankun pouch, framed by the tattered remains of a golden net hanging in the branches above—clearly dropped by some unlucky cultivator who’d torn themselves loose in a panic. Wei Wuxian picked up the pouch and emptied it. It held a standard assortment of hunting gear: gourds of medicinal wine, warding talismans, a small demon-revealing mirror, and assorted oddities.

Flipping through the scraps, he casually pulled out a yellow paper charm, only for it to instantly burst into flames in his fingers!

It was an Incinerating Ward—designed to feed on dark energy. The moment it encountered yin energy, it ignited; the thicker the resentment, the fiercer the blaze. Igniting the second it left the pouch meant a malicious spirit was lurking right on top of him.

Dropping into a guarded stance, Wei Wuxian held the burning scrap up, sweeping it to test the direction. Pointing east, the flame guttered; turning west, the fire surged high. He took several cautious steps in that direction until a hunched, pale silhouette materialized beneath the branches of an old pine.

The talisman burned down to ash, drifting through his fingers. An elderly man stood with his back turned, muttering endlessly to himself.

Wei Wuxian crept closer until the broken whispers became clear.

“It hurts… It hurts so bad…”

Wei Wuxian murmured, “Where does it hurt?”

“My head… my head. My head hurts…”

“Let me see,” Wei Wuxian said gently.

He stepped around to the old man’s side. Right in the center of the spirit's forehead was a gaping, blood-crusted crater.

A deceased spirit.

He had likely been murdered by a blunt blow to the skull. But the spirit was draped in traditional burial shrouds—fine silk, beautifully tailored—indicating he had been formally washed, shrouded, and properly interred in a ancestral plot.

This was not a living soul torn from a mortal body.

Yet on Dafan Mountain, an old grave-spirit like this had no business wandering the woods.

The pieces didn't fit, and a creeping sense of dread settled into Wei Wuxian’s gut. He vaulted onto the donkey's back, slapped its rump, and spurred the animal up the trail toward the path Jin Ling and the juniors had taken.

Higher up, several cultivators were lingering near the old burial mounds, hoping to wait the beast out. Someone had boldly planted a Spirit Attraction Flag, but the only thing it reeled in was a flock of weeping, harmless graveyard specters.

Wei Wuxian reined in the beast, sweeping his gaze across the clearing. “Excuse me! Quick question—which way did the young masters from the Jin and Lan clans go?”

Washing his face had worked wonders; now that he looked like a human being, someone actually answered him. “They cleared out of here a while ago. Headed up to the Goddess Temple.”

Wei Wuxian’s eyes narrowed. “The Goddess Temple?”

The ragged family of rogue cultivators, having realized the nets were gone, had crept back up the slopes and was mingling with the crowd. The middle-aged leader spotted the donkey and the clothes, recognizing the crazy savior who had rescued them earlier. Feeling awkward, he pretended not to notice, but the sweet, round-faced girl pointed up the trail for him: “Over that way! It’s a stone grotto shrine built into the cliffside.”

Wei Wuxian pressed, “What kind of deity is enshrined there?”

The girl stammered, “I… I think it’s a natural stone statue of a Heavenly Maiden.”

Wei Wuxian offered a curt nod. “Much obliged.”

Without another word, he kicked the donkey into a dead sprint toward the grotto.

A deadbeat getting married.
Lightning splitting an ancestral coffin.
A fiancé mauled by mountain wolves.
A father and daughter hollowed out one after the other…
And a ghost draped in lavish burial silks.

The scattered clues clicked together, forming a single, terrifying line.

No wonder the Compasses of Evil couldn't lock onto a bearing. No wonder the Spirit Attraction Flags were useless.

Every cultivator on this peak had underestimated what was hunting Dafan Mountain.

It wasn't a phantom, and it wasn't a beast.

It was something entirely different.
